newsitem.title: SWITZERLAND: FOCUS - German carmakers off to strong start in 1997.
newsitem.headline: FOCUS - German carmakers off to strong start in 1997.

text.p: Nearly a million car buyers around the world put their money down on German vehicles during the first two months of 1997, enabling three major German carmakers on Tuesday to report robust growth in international sales.

The top carmakers -- Mercedes-Benz AG, Volkswagen AG and BMW AG -- said at the Geneva car show that sales were off to a strong start despite concerns about the German market and little consumer spending.
Although many industry executives declined to predict that the robust growth would keep up for the balance of the year, many said they were cautiously optimistic for more gains.

Juergen Hubbert, the Mercedes management board member in charge of passenger vehicle sales, told journalists late on Monday that the Stuttgart-based carmaker saw sales in January and February rise five percent over year-ago levels.
"The signs appear good that we will clearly be able to increase our sales" over 1996 when the luxury carmaker sold 645,000 vehicles around the world," Hubbert said.
BMW, the Munich-based carmaker said on Tuesday that customer sales in January and February were up 17 percent to more than 100,000 vehicles over the 1996 period.
But BMW also said sales at its Rover group in Britain were not up to year-ago levels during the two-month period, in part due to the introduction of two new models.

BMW management board chairman Bernd Pischetsrieder, in the text of a speech to be delivered at a BMW event on Tuesday night at the Geneva car show, said the carmaker expected a "stable development" in BMW sales at higher levels.
"If the January and February figures show us a positive direction, then we would expect for all of 1997 with sales of BMW vehicles a stable development at higher levels," he said.

Volkswagen AG, considered the largest carmaker in Europe, said on Tuesday that group sales rose 13 percent to about 660,000 vehicles in February and that sales so far for the year were doing well. The Wolfsburg-based carmaker last week reported an 18 percent increase in January sales.

VW management board member Robert Buechelhofer told Reuters in an interview that sales in the critical west European market were up about seven to eight percent for February compared with the 1996 year-ago period.

But he said sales were down about four to six percent in Germany during February, in part due to the suspension of production for about a week of VW's Polo model due to parts shortages caused by the Spanish truckers' strike.
Buechelhofer however noted that incoming orders in Germany for the first two months of 1997 were up 30 percent and that he expected the sales situation to stabilise in the country.
"Incoming orders in Germany are going very well and have been above our expectations," he said. "The situation in Germany will work itself out."
He declined to provide forecasts for 1997 VW sales, saying "it would be speculative to talk about the full year".
But Buechelhofer said he expected VW to maintain the worldwide market share of about 10 percent achieved in 1996 also in 1997 despite weakening consumer demand for vehicles.

VW said provisional sales results for February showed further success in its international expansion, with sales up 30 percent in eastern European and North American sales up 27 percent as a result of its massive marketing efforts.
In South America and Africa, VW said sales were up 17 percent and that sales in the Asia-Pacific region rose 28 percent, including a 34 percent increase in sales in Japan.
Among VW's global brands, Buechelhofer said VW passenger car sales to customers during February rose 10 percent but fell four to six percent in Germany.

VW's luxury brand Audi reported a 28 percent rise in sales for February. Incoming Audi chief executive Franz-Josef Paefgen later told Reuters he was optimistic that Audi's 1997 sales would top 500,000 vehicles. The 1996 sales were 492,000.
